implementation_notes: The temporal collection is three lines: BTreeMap's ordered API answers the read directly - history.range(..=at).next_back().map(|(_, v)| v) is the latest version whose effective start is not after `at` - and chrono::NaiveDate (or time::Date) is the Time Point as a plain ordered Copy value; slice::partition_point does the same over a Vec<(NaiveDate, T)> kept sorted when the history is small or the cache behaviour matters. What replaces the classic structure: the ordered map plus one method; the owner stays a struct with at(when) and a current() shortcut, the put protocol is insert plus, for a retroactive insertion, removal/re-insertion of the superseded milestones, and the bitemporal-runtime crate covers the two-dimensional case. The explicit Effectivity range struct is still justified when validity can have gaps - a start-date-keyed map cannot represent 'no value in force'.
pitfalls: BTreeMap::insert at an existing key silently replaces the version, so a second change on the same date leaves no trace; a revision key (BTreeMap<(NaiveDate, u64), T>) or a second time dimension is required for that granularity.

range(..=when) is only correct when the lookup value has the same type and granularity as the keys: mixing DateTime<Utc> keys with NaiveDate lookups needs an explicit conversion, and NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt returns Option (unwrapping user input panics).

Returning Option<&Money> borrows the whole struct, so any mutation after a read needs an owned/cloned value or interior mutability (RefCell/RwLock), which is where the convenience often breaks in practice.

Float values make the ordering non-total (NaN compares false with everything, so range() misbehaves): store minor units as integers or a decimal type, and remember that NaiveDate has no time-zone, so it must be derived from a zone-aware instant deliberately.
